artworks.title: Aethra Showing her Son Theseus the Place Where his Father had Hidden his Arms
artworks.description: In this French Neoclassical history painting, Aethra, princess of Troezen and mother of Theseus, leads her grown son to the great rock under which his absent father Aegeus had hidden a sword and a pair of sandals. When the youth proved strong enough to roll the stone aside and recover these tokens, he was ready to claim his birthright in Athens. Brenet stages the moment of revelation as a tender, dramatic gesture, casting Aethra in her defining maternal role as the keeper of the secret that launches the hero's journey.

artworks.title: Theseus Finding his Father's Sword (Thésée retrouve l'épée de son père)
artworks.description: Set within a classical architectural landscape, this Baroque canvas depicts Theseus lifting the boulder to discover the sword and sandals left by Aegeus, while his mother Aethra stands beside him, having guided him to the spot. Painted with Jean Lemaire's grand architectural framework, Poussin presents the recognition scene with measured gravity: Aethra's presence anchors the episode as a coming-of-age rite, the mother witnessing her son seize the proof of his royal parentage before he sets out for Athens.

artworks.title: Theseus Discovering his Father's Sword
artworks.description: The Venetian late-Baroque painter Antonio Balestra shows the muscular young Theseus straining to heave aside the rock that conceals his father's hidden arms, his mother Aethra at his side directing him to the treasure. The dynamic diagonal composition and warm Venetian palette dramatize the heroic effort, but it is Aethra who supplies the narrative key: only she knew where Aegeus laid the tokens, and the painting renders her as the indispensable witness to her son's first feat of strength.

artworks.title: Demophon Freeing Aethra (Attic white-ground kylix)
artworks.description: This ancient Athenian white-ground cup, now in the Staatliche Antikensammlungen in Munich, illustrates the other great episode of Aethra's life: her old age as a captive at Troy. Having been carried off by the Dioscuri in retaliation for Theseus' abduction of Helen, the aged Aethra served as Helen's handmaid until, at the fall of Troy, her grandsons Demophon and Acamas recognized and rescued her. The vase captures the freeing of the white-haired queen, a beloved Athenian subject that completes her story as both mother of a hero and grandmother delivered from bondage.
